1.1: From my grandfather: good character and keeping my temper under control.
1.2: From my father's memory: modesty and a manly, upright character.
1.3: From my mother: kindness, generosity, not even thinking of doing wrong, and living simply rather than like the rich.
1.4: From my great-grandfather: get good teachers at home and don't be stingy about spending on education.
1.5: From my tutor: don't be a sports fanatic, work hard, need little, do things yourself, mind your own business and ignore gossip.
1.6: From Diognetus: don't waste time on trivia, superstition or con artists, put up with people speaking freely, and take philosophy seriously.
1.7: From Rusticus: work on your character, skip showing off and fancy talk, write plainly, forgive easily, and read deeply instead of skimming.
1.8: From Apollonius: think for yourself, stay steady through pain and grief, be firm yet flexible, and accept favors without fawning or ignoring them.
1.9: From Sextus: be kind, live by nature, look after friends, be patient with fools, and stay calm and warm without making a show of it.
1.10: From Alexander the grammarian: don't nitpick people's mistakes in public; just model the right way tactfully.
1.11: From Fronto: notice the envy and hypocrisy that come with power, and how cold the upper class can be toward their own.
1.12: From Alexander the Platonist: don't keep telling people you're too busy as an excuse to dodge your duties to them.
1.13: From Catulus: take a friend's criticism seriously even when it's unfair, praise your teachers, and truly love your children.
1.14: From my brother Severus: love family, truth and justice, believe in equal rights and free speech, be generous and say plainly what you think.
1.15: From Maximus: self-control, cheerfulness even when ill, doing your job without complaining, and being honest, unhurried and calm.
1.16: What I admired in my adoptive father: calm, steady judgment, no vanity, hard work, listening to advice, simple habits, and enjoying or giving up pleasures with equal ease.
1.17: I'm grateful to the gods for good family, teachers and friends, for being spared temptations, and for luck that kept me on the right path.
2.1: Each morning, expect to meet rude, ungrateful, selfish people; they act from ignorance, they can't really harm me, and we're made to work together, not fight.
2.2: You're just flesh, breath and a mind; stop being jerked around like a puppet, and stop resenting the present or dreading the future.
2.3: Everything that happens is part of a providential whole and good for it; settle on these principles and stop craving more books, so you die grateful.
2.4: You keep putting off what matters; your time is limited, and if you don't use it to clear your head, it will be gone for good.
2.5: Do each thing as if it were the last act of your life, with focus, dignity and kindness; a calm life needs only a few principles.
2.6: Keep hurting yourself, soul, by hanging your happiness on other people's opinions; you're running out of time to respect yourself.
2.7: Don't let outside events whirl you around; but don't fill life with pointless busyness either; have a clear aim for what you do.
2.8: People are rarely made miserable by not knowing what others think, but always by not paying attention to their own minds.
2.9: Remember you're part of a larger whole, and nobody can stop you from acting in line with that nature.
2.10: Wrongs done out of desire are worse than wrongs done out of anger, because pleasure drags you willingly while anger at least stings.
2.11: Act as if you could die any moment; death is nothing to fear, since only vice is truly bad, and that's always within your power to avoid.
2.12: Everything vanishes fast, and so does the memory of it; pleasures, fame and pain are worthless, and fearing death, a natural process, is childish.
2.13: Stop prying into everything and guessing what others think; looking after your own inner self is enough.
2.14: You only ever lose the present moment, so a long life and a short one come to the same; the present is all anyone has.
2.15: Everything is opinion; it's how you judge things that shapes them.
2.16: You harm your own soul by resenting events, by anger at people, by giving in to pleasure or pain, by faking, and by acting without purpose.
2.17: Life is short, the body decays, and fame fades into oblivion; only philosophy can guide you: keep your inner self calm, honest and purposeful, and accept change.
3.1: Hurry: not just because death gets closer daily, but because your mind may fail before your body does.
3.2: Even nature's side effects, like cracked bread crust, split figs or an old face, have their own beauty if you look with the right eye.
3.3: Famous doctors, prophets, conquerors and philosophers all died anyway; you've made the voyage, so step off the boat without fear.
3.4: Don't waste your remaining life wondering what others are doing or thinking; keep your thoughts clean enough that you could share them openly.
3.5: Work willingly for the common good, say little, don't overcommit, and stand on your own feet instead of relying on others to prop you up.
3.6: If you find anything better than a just, honest, self-controlled mind, go for it; if not, don't let fame, power or pleasure crowd it out.
3.7: Never value anything that would make you break your word, lose your self-respect, hate, deceive or hide; such a person neither chases nor fears death.
3.8: A purified mind has nothing rotten hidden in it, nothing servile or fake, and its life is complete whenever it ends.
3.9: Guard your power to form judgments; on it depends whether you think clearly, treat people well and accept what the gods send.
3.10: Hold on to a few essentials; you only live in the present moment, life is short, and fame after death is tiny and fleeting.
3.11: Define and strip down whatever you face to see what it really is and what it's worth; seeing things clearly gives you greatness of mind.
3.12: Do the task in front of you seriously and calmly, expecting nothing and fearing nothing, speaking the truth, and you'll be happy; no one can stop you.
3.13: Like a doctor with tools always at hand, keep your principles ready so you're prepared for whatever comes up.
3.14: Stop drifting and saving things for later; you won't get to them. Drop false hopes and help yourself while you still can.
3.15: People don't realize how much ordinary words like stealing, sowing or buying mean; seeing what should be done takes inner vision, not eyes.
3.16: Animals feel, beasts and tyrants follow desire, and even traitors can reason; what marks a good person is contentment with their lot and an undisturbed, honest mind.
4.1: A healthy mind adapts to whatever happens and turns obstacles into fuel, like a strong fire that burns whatever is thrown on it and grows higher.
4.2: Don't do anything aimlessly or carelessly; act with purpose and skill.
4.3: You don't need a vacation to find peace; you can retreat into your own mind anytime. Things don't disturb us, our opinions do, and everything changes.
4.4: If we all share reason, we share one law and are fellow citizens; the whole world is in a sense one state.
4.5: Death is a natural mystery like birth, just elements coming apart; nothing to be ashamed of.
4.6: Bad people will act badly; expecting otherwise is like expecting a fig tree without sap. Soon you and they will both be dead and forgotten.
4.7: Drop the opinion 'I've been harmed,' and the harm is gone.
4.8: What doesn't make you a worse person doesn't make your life worse or harm you.
4.9: What's good for the whole had to happen this way.
4.10: Everything that happens happens justly if you look closely; in all you do, focus on being good.
4.11: Don't see things the way the person who wronged you sees them, or wants you to; see them as they really are.
4.12: Do only what reason says helps people, and change your mind when someone shows you you're wrong, but for good reasons, not for pleasure or reputation.
4.13: You have reason; then use it. If it's doing its job, what more do you want?
4.14: You came from nature as a part of it, and you'll be absorbed back into it.
4.15: Like grains of incense on one altar, one falls first and another later; it makes no difference.
4.16: Go back to your principles and within ten days people who now think you're an animal will think you're a god.
4.17: Don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you're alive and able, be good.
4.18: You save so much trouble by not watching what your neighbor says or does, and just making sure your own actions are right.
4.19: Craving fame after death is pointless: everyone who remembers you will die soon, and even eternal praise means nothing to you.
4.20: Beautiful things are beautiful in themselves; praise doesn't make anything better and blame doesn't make it worse.
4.21: Just as the earth makes room for the dead by transforming bodies, souls may dissolve into the universe; nature recycles everything.
4.22: Don't get swept around; in every action aim at justice, and in every impression keep your understanding clear.
4.23: Whatever suits the universe suits me; nothing is too early or too late if its time is right. Everything comes from nature and returns to it.
4.24: Most of what we say and do is unnecessary; cut it out, ask 'is this necessary?', and you'll have more calm and more time.
4.25: Try living as a good person who is content with their share and with their own fair, kind actions, and see how it suits you.
4.26: Don't get upset; keep it simple. If someone does wrong, they harm themselves. Life is short, so use the present well.
4.27: Whether the universe is ordered or chaos, it's still a whole; how can you keep order inside yourself and expect disorder outside?
4.28: A list of bad characters: dark, weak, stubborn, brutish, childish, stupid, fake, crude, deceitful, tyrannical.
4.29: Resenting what happens cuts you off from nature; running from reason makes you a fugitive, and needing others for everything makes you poor.
4.30: One philosopher has no tunic, another no books, yet they stick to reason even when it doesn't pay.
4.31: Love the craft you've learned, however humble, and live trusting the gods, being neither anyone's tyrant nor their slave.
4.32: Look back at any era: people marrying, fighting, scheming, grumbling, and all of them gone now. Don't wear yourself out over trivia.
4.33: Even the most famous names become outdated and forgotten; what matters is fair thoughts, helpful acts, honest words and accepting what happens.
4.34: Let fate spin your life into whatever she wants, and go along willingly.
4.35: Everything lasts only a day, both the one who remembers and the one remembered.
4.36: Everything happens through change; nature loves nothing more than transforming things, and everything that exists is the seed of what comes next.
4.37: You'll die soon, and you're still not simple, calm, kind to everyone or wise enough to see that only acting justly counts.
4.38: Study what drives people, even wise people: what they avoid and what they chase.
4.39: Harm isn't in other people or in your body; it's in your opinion about things. Stop judging things as bad and all is well.
4.40: Think of the universe as one living being with one soul, where everything is connected and causes everything else.
4.41: You're a little soul carrying around a corpse.
4.42: Change isn't bad for things, and existing as a result of change isn't good; it's just how nature works.
4.43: Time is a rushing river of events: as soon as something appears it's swept away, and the next thing too.
4.44: Illness, death, slander and betrayal are as ordinary and expected as roses in spring; don't be shocked by them.
4.45: Events aren't a random list; each fits rationally with what came before, in a wonderful connected order.
4.46: Don't live like you're asleep or just repeat what you were taught; people quarrel with the very reason that runs the universe.
4.47: If you knew you'd die tomorrow or the day after, you wouldn't care which; dying years from now instead is no bigger a deal.
4.48: Doctors, astrologers, philosophers, heroes and whole cities are all dead; pass through this brief life naturally and leave it content, like a ripe olive falling.
4.49: Be like a rock the waves crash against: it stands firm. Don't say 'I'm unlucky this happened'; say 'I'm lucky I can bear it well.'
4.50: People who clung to life ended up in the grave just the same; against infinite time, three days and three lifetimes are the same.
4.51: Always take the short way, which is the natural way: say and do what is soundest, and you'll be free of trouble and pretense.
5.1: When you don't want to get out of bed in the morning, remember you're getting up to do the work you were made for; plants, birds and bees all do their part, so why should you lie under the covers?
5.2: How easy it is to push away any troubling thought and be at peace right away.
5.3: If something is right to say or do, do it, and ignore other people's criticism; they follow their own minds, so keep going your own way.
5.4: I'll keep living by nature until I fall and rest, returning my breath to the air and my body to the earth that fed me all my life.
5.5: Maybe you're not brilliant, but you can still be honest, serious, hard-working, content, kind and free of whining; no lack of talent excuses falling short there.
5.6: Do good without keeping score or seeking credit, like a vine producing grapes and then simply producing more next season.
5.7: Prayers should be simple and for everyone, like the Athenians asking Zeus to rain on all their fields.
5.8: Accept what nature hands you, even illness or loss, the way you'd accept a doctor's prescription; it fits the whole and serves the health of the universe.
5.9: Don't get discouraged when you fail to live by your principles; just come back to them, the way you'd return to a soothing remedy, not a harsh teacher.
5.10: Things are murky, people are hard to bear and everything is in flux; wait calmly for the end, knowing nothing happens against nature and no one can make me act against my conscience.
5.11: Keep asking yourself what you're using your mind for right now, and whose soul you have at the moment: a child's, a tyrant's, an animal's?
5.12: Notice how people mock wealth and luxury as 'too much stuff' but would never mock real virtues; that tells you what is truly good.
5.13: I'm made of matter and form, and neither will vanish; every part of me will change into another part of the universe, forever.
5.14: Reason is self-sufficient: it starts from its own principles and moves straight toward its goal, which is why right actions are called 'right-road' acts.
5.15: Things that don't belong to us as human beings aren't what make us good; the more someone does without them, or bears losing them, the better a person they are.
5.16: Your mind takes on the color of your habitual thoughts, so dye it with good ones: wherever you can live, you can live well, even in a palace.
5.17: It's madness to expect the impossible, and it's impossible that bad people won't do bad things.
5.18: Nothing happens to anyone that they weren't made able to bear; others endure the same things calmly, out of ignorance or pride, so wisdom should do at least as well.
5.19: Things can't touch the mind at all; the mind moves itself, and how it judges determines how things appear to it.
5.20: People who block me become like weather or wild animals; they can stop my actions but not my mind, which turns every obstacle into a way forward. What stands in the way becomes the way.
5.21: Respect the best power in the universe, the one that directs everything, and respect the same kind of power in yourself, which directs your life.
5.22: If it doesn't hurt the community, it doesn't hurt me; and if it does, don't get angry at the person, show them their mistake.
5.23: Everything is passing away like a river; the past and future are a bottomless abyss, so it's foolish to be proud of things or tormented by them.
5.24: Remember how tiny your share is of all matter, all time and all fate.
5.25: Someone wronged me? That's their business. I have what nature wants me to have and I'm doing what my nature wants me to do.
5.26: Don't let your mind get tangled up in physical pleasure or pain; you'll feel the sensation, which is natural, but don't add the judgment that it's good or bad.
5.27: Live with the gods by being content with what you're given and following the inner divine guide, your own reason.
5.28: Why get angry at someone who smells bad? Anger doesn't help. Use your reason to show them their fault calmly; if they listen, they're fixed and anger was never needed.
5.29: You can live here the way you'd want to live in a better place; if people won't let you, leave without complaint, like walking out of a smoky room.
5.30: The universe's intelligence is social: it arranges everything in its proper place and fits the best things together in harmony.
5.31: Look back on how you've treated family, friends, teachers and servants; count what you've endured, the beauty you've seen, and the kindness you've shown to difficult people.
5.32: Why should ignorant people disturb someone who understands? Real understanding knows the beginning and end and the reason running through everything.
5.33: Soon you'll be ashes and a forgotten name; what people chase is empty, like puppies fighting or children crying. Until then, honor the gods, do good, and be patient.
5.34: You can live with a steady flow of happiness if you think and act rightly: don't let others block you, and find your good in being just.
5.35: If it's not my fault and the community isn't hurt, why am I bothered by it?
5.36: Help people, but don't treat their loss of trivial things as a real disaster; good fortune is simply a good character, good feelings and good actions.
6.1: The universe's material is pliable and the reason that runs it means no harm; everything is made and finished according to it.
6.2: Whether you're cold or warm, tired or rested, criticized or praised, even dying, just do your duty well; dying is one of life's tasks too.
6.3: Look beneath the surface; don't let any thing's real nature or worth slip past you.
6.4: Everything around you will soon change, turning to vapor or scattering apart.
6.5: Your guiding mind knows its own state, what it's doing, and what it's working with.
6.6: The best revenge is not to be like the person who wronged you.
6.7: Find your joy and rest in one thing: moving from one act of service to the next, with God in mind.
6.8: The mind wakes and steers itself, shapes itself as it wants, and makes whatever happens appear the way it chooses.
6.9: Everything is carried out according to the one nature of the universe, not some other nature outside or inside it.
6.10: Either the world is random atoms or there's order and providence; if random, why stay or care, and if ordered, I can honor it, stand firm and trust.
6.11: When circumstances throw you off balance, get back to yourself fast; the more often you return to your rhythm, the better you'll master it.
6.12: Treat your job like a stepmother and philosophy like your mother: do your duty but keep returning to philosophy, which makes work bearable and you bearable at work.
6.13: See things stripped bare: fancy food is a dead fish, fine wine is grape juice, a royal robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Strip away the hype that makes things look important.
6.14: Most people admire things like stone, plants or animals, or skill and slaves; the wise value only a rational, social soul and keep their own in that state.
6.15: Things rush into and out of existence like a stream; caring deeply about any of them is like falling in love with a sparrow that's already flown past.
6.16: Applause and fame are just clapping tongues; what's worth valuing is acting by your own nature, the way any good craft aims at its purpose. Respect your own mind and you'll be content.
6.17: The elements move up, down and around, but virtue moves on a quieter, more divine road and goes happily along it.
6.18: People won't praise those around them but crave praise from future generations they'll never meet; that's as silly as being upset that earlier people didn't praise you.
6.19: Just because something is hard for you doesn't mean it's impossible; if a human can do it, so can you.
6.20: When someone scratches you in a sports match, you don't hold a grudge; you just watch out for them. Give people that same easy pass in the rest of life.
6.21: If someone can show me I'm wrong, I'll gladly change; truth never hurt anyone, but staying in error does.
6.22: I do my duty and don't let other things bother me; they're lifeless, unreasoning, or lost.
6.23: Use animals and things generously, treat people with fellowship, and turn to the gods; even three hours lived like that is enough.
6.24: Alexander the Great and his stable boy ended up the same after death.
6.25: So much happens inside one body at once that it shouldn't surprise you that everything in the universe exists together.
6.26: If you're spelling a name and people get angry, you don't shout back; you calmly finish the letters. Do the same with every duty: follow the steps and don't react to angry people.
6.27: People do wrong because they think it's good for them; instead of getting irritated, teach them and show them, without anger.
6.28: Death is the end of being pulled around by senses, impulses, restless thoughts and the body's demands.
6.29: It's shameful for your spirit to give up while your body is still going.
6.30: Don't let power go to your head. Stay simple, good, honest, kind and hardworking, like the mentor you admired; life is short and its only fruit is good character and serving others.
6.31: Wake up and come to your senses: the things troubling you now are like the dreams you just woke from.
6.32: Only my own thoughts and actions in the present are truly in my power; everything else, including my body, past and future, is neutral.
6.33: Work isn't against nature as long as it's the right kind of work for you, so labor isn't a bad thing.
6.34: Robbers, murderers and tyrants have enjoyed plenty of pleasures, so pleasure can't be the good.
6.35: Craftsmen and doctors won't compromise the principles of their trade; it's strange if a person respects their own reason less.
6.36: Continents, oceans and mountains are tiny next to the universe, and all of time is a point in eternity. Even the harmful things, like thorns and poison, come from the same source as the beautiful.
6.37: Whoever has seen the present has seen everything; all of history is the same in kind and form.
6.38: Think often about how everything in the universe is connected and woven together in one order.
6.39: Accept the circumstances you've been given, and love the people you've ended up with, sincerely.
6.40: A tool's maker isn't inside it, but the power that made living things stays within them, so respect it and live by it.
6.41: If you call things outside your control good or bad, you'll blame the gods and resent people when you lose them; judge only what's in your power and there's no reason for that.
6.42: We're all working toward one end, some knowingly, some not, even the complainers; just make sure you're a worthwhile part, not the throwaway line in the play.
6.43: The sun doesn't try to be the rain; each star is different but they all work together to the same end.
6.44: Whether the gods planned my life or only the whole, it's for the good, so accept it. My nature is rational and social: my city is Rome, but as a human, my country is the world.
6.45: Whatever happens to someone serves the whole, and what helps one person generally helps others too.
6.46: Like a show you've seen too many times, life repeats the same things over and over. How long will this go on?
6.47: Think of all the great orators, philosophers, scientists and heroes who are long dead; only one thing really matters: living in truth and justice, kind even to liars and wrongdoers.
6.48: When you want to feel cheerful, think of the good qualities of people around you: one's energy, another's modesty, another's generosity.
6.49: You're not upset that you weigh what you weigh and not three hundred pounds, so don't be upset that your lifespan has its limits.
6.50: Try to persuade people, but do what's right even against their will; if someone forcibly blocks you, accept it calmly and use the obstacle to practice another virtue.
6.51: Lovers of fame put their good in other people's actions, lovers of pleasure in their sensations, but wise people put it in their own actions.
6.52: You don't have to form an opinion about something or be disturbed by it; things can't force judgments on you.
6.53: Get in the habit of listening closely to others and trying to see from inside their mind.
6.54: What's not good for the hive isn't good for the bee.
6.55: If sailors insulted the captain or patients the doctor, who would they listen to, and how could they be saved?
6.56: How many people I came into the world with have already left it.
6.57: Honey tastes bitter to the sick and kids love a ball; false opinions distort us just as strongly, so why be angry at people who have them?
6.58: No one can stop you from living by your own nature, and nothing happens to you against the nature of the universe.
6.59: Think about who people are trying to please, for what and how; time will soon bury it all, as it already has so much.
7.1: Whatever bad thing happens, you've seen it before; history, cities and homes are full of the same stuff. Nothing is new, and nothing lasts.
7.2: Your principles only die if you let the thoughts behind them go out, and you can always rekindle them; to get your life back, just start seeing things the way you used to.
7.3: Life is a show of parades, puppies fighting over a bone and ants hauling loads; take it with good humor, knowing a person is worth what they spend their energy on.
7.4: When people talk, pay attention to what they mean; when they act, watch what they're aiming at.
7.5: If I'm up to a task, I do it; if not, I hand it to someone better or do my best with help, aiming only at what's useful for everyone.
7.6: Many who were famous are forgotten, and many who praised the famous are long dead.
7.7: Don't be ashamed to accept help; like a wounded soldier climbing a wall, what matters is getting your job done.
7.8: Don't let the future worry you; you'll face it, if you have to, with the same reason you use now.
7.9: Everything is woven together by a sacred bond; there is one universe, one god, one substance, one law, one reason and one truth.
7.10: All matter soon dissolves into the whole, every cause returns to universal reason, and every memory is soon buried by time.
7.11: For a rational being, acting by nature and acting by reason are the same thing.
7.12: Stand up straight, or be set straight by others.
7.13: We're limbs of one body of rational beings, not just separate parts; if you don't feel that, you're doing good out of duty instead of from the heart.
7.14: Let whatever happens hit the parts of me that can feel it; I'm not harmed unless I judge it to be bad, and I don't have to.
7.15: Whatever anyone says or does, I have to be good, like an emerald that keeps its color no matter what.
7.16: The mind never scares or hurts itself; it needs nothing unless it invents a need, so it stays calm and free unless it gets in its own way.
7.17: Happiness means having a good spirit inside; so, troubling thought, go away, I don't want you. I'm not angry, just leave.
7.18: Afraid of change? Nothing happens without it: you can't take a hot bath or eat a meal without something changing, and your own change is just as natural and necessary.
7.19: Everything is swept along in the universe like a rushing river; time has already swallowed countless great thinkers, and it will do the same to everyone.
7.20: The only thing that worries me is doing something human nature doesn't allow, or doing it the wrong way or at the wrong time.
7.21: Soon you'll forget everything, and soon everyone will forget you.
7.22: It's human to love even people who wrong you, once you remember they're family, they acted out of ignorance, you'll both die soon, and they didn't really hurt your mind.
7.23: Nature molds everything like wax: a horse, then a tree, then a person, each lasting only briefly, and being broken down is no harder than being put together.
7.24: Constant scowling kills your looks for good, and that shows it's against reason too.
7.25: Nature will soon transform everything you see into new things, and those into others, so the world stays forever new.
7.26: When someone wrongs you, figure out what they thought was good or bad; you'll pity them instead of being angry or surprised, and forgiving them gets easier.
7.27: Focus on what you have rather than what you don't, and imagine how much you'd miss your best things; just don't get so attached that losing them would wreck you.
7.28: Withdraw into yourself; your reason is content with itself when it acts justly, and that brings peace.
7.29: Erase false impressions, stop being jerked around, stay in the present, understand what's happening, think of your last hour, and leave someone's wrong where it happened.
7.30: Pay close attention to what is said, and get your mind inside what's happening and why.
7.31: Be simple and modest, stay indifferent to things that are neither good nor bad, love people and follow God; remember that law rules everything.
7.32: Death is either scattering, breaking into atoms, or nothingness; in any case it's an ending or a change.
7.33: Unbearable pain ends quickly, and lasting pain is bearable; the mind can keep its calm by withdrawing into itself, and it isn't made worse.
7.34: Look at the people chasing fame; just as new sand buries old sand, each event in life is soon covered by the next.
7.35: Someone who sees all of time and existence can't think one human life is a big deal, so they won't think death is bad either.
7.36: It's kingly to do good and be badly spoken of for it.
7.37: It's shameful that your face obeys your mind's commands while your mind can't keep itself in order.
7.38: Don't get angry at things; they don't care.
7.39: May we bring joy to the gods and ourselves.
7.40: Lives are harvested like ripe grain: one person is born, another dies.
7.41: If the gods don't look after me and my children, there's a reason for that too.
7.42: I have what is good and just on my side.
7.43: Don't join in others' wailing, and don't get swept away by emotion.
7.44: A good person doesn't calculate the risk of living or dying; they only ask whether what they're doing is right or wrong.
7.45: Wherever you've taken your stand, or been stationed, stay there and face the danger; desertion is worse than death or anything else.
7.46: Being noble isn't the same as staying alive; a real person shouldn't cling to life but leave their lifespan to God and ask how best to live the time they have.
7.47: Watch the stars move as if you're traveling with them, and think about the elements changing into each other; it washes off the grime of everyday life.
7.48: Look at human affairs as if from above: crowds, armies, farms, weddings, births, deaths, courts, feasts and markets, all mixed together.
7.49: Look at past empires rising and falling and you can predict the future; forty years of watching human life is as good as ten thousand.
7.50: What comes from the earth goes back to the earth, and what comes from heaven returns there; death is just elements coming apart.
7.51: People try food, drink and magic to escape death, but we must take the wind heaven sends and work without complaining.
7.52: Someone might be a better wrestler than you, but that doesn't make them more kind, modest, disciplined or forgiving.
7.53: If you're doing work in line with the reason gods and people share, there's nothing to fear.
7.54: Anywhere, anytime, you can accept your situation, treat the people around you fairly, and check your thoughts before letting them in.
7.55: Don't study other people's minds; look where nature is leading you. Your first duty is to be social, then to not give in to the body, and then to avoid error.
7.56: Imagine you've already died and your life is over; live whatever extra time you get according to nature.
7.57: Love only what happens to you, what fate weaves for you; what could suit you better?
7.58: When something happens, remember people who complained about the same thing; where are they now? Don't copy them; use what happens as material to work with and just be good.
7.59: Look within: there's a fountain of good inside you that will keep flowing if you keep digging.
7.60: Carry your body steadily and composed, the way an intelligent face does, but without putting on airs.
7.61: Living well is more like wrestling than dancing: you have to stand ready and steady for sudden, unexpected attacks.
7.62: Look at the people whose approval you want and how their minds work; you won't blame them for their errors, and you won't want their approval.
7.63: Nobody is wrong on purpose; everyone who lacks truth, justice or kindness lacks it unwillingly, so be gentler with everyone.
7.64: Pain doesn't disgrace you or damage your mind; it's never both unbearable and endless if you don't add to it in your head. Even irritations like heat or tiredness are just pain you're giving in to.
7.65: Don't treat cruel people the way they treat others.
7.66: Fame and dramatic acts don't prove Socrates was good; what counts is whether his soul was just, pious, unbothered by others' wickedness and calm about whatever happened.
7.67: You can be a godlike person whom no one recognizes, and very little is needed to be happy; even if you'll never be an expert, you can still be free, modest, kind and obedient to God.
7.68: You can stay calm and free even if everyone shouts at you or wild beasts tear you apart; your mind can see each thing for what it is and use whatever happens as material for virtue.
7.69: A perfect character lives each day as if it were the last, without frenzy, laziness or pretense.
7.70: The gods aren't fed up with putting up with bad people forever, and even care for them; you'll be gone soon, and you're one of the bad ones, so why are you tired of it?
7.71: It's silly to try to escape other people's flaws, which is impossible, instead of your own, which you can.
7.72: Whatever isn't rational or social, a rational and social mind rightly sees as beneath it.
7.73: When you've done someone a good turn, why look for something extra like credit or payback, the way fools do?
7.74: Nobody gets tired of being helped, and acting by nature is help; so don't get tired of helping yourself by helping others.
7.75: Nature set the universe in motion and everything follows from that; remembering it will calm you about many things.
8.1: You can't claim you lived your whole life as a philosopher, so stop worrying how you look to others; just live the rest as your nature wants. You've wandered everywhere looking for happiness and it was in doing what human nature requires.
8.2: Before every action ask: will I regret this? Soon I'll be dead; if what I'm doing is the work of a thinking, social being, what more do I need?
8.3: Conquerors like Alexander and Caesar were slaves to countless worries, while Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates understood how things really are.
8.4: People will keep doing the same things even if you burst with frustration.
8.5: First, don't get upset; everything follows nature, and soon you'll be nobody, like the emperors before you. Then focus on your task and do it as a good person, speaking justly, kindly and honestly.
8.6: Nature's job is to move things around and transform them; everything changes, but there's nothing new to fear.
8.7: A rational mind is doing well when it accepts nothing false, acts only for the common good, wants only what's in its power, and welcomes what nature assigns it.
8.8: You may not have time to read, but you have time to curb your arrogance, rise above pleasure, pain and fame, and not be annoyed by stupid, ungrateful people, even to care for them.
8.9: Stop complaining, out loud, about your job or your life.
8.10: Nobody regrets passing up a pleasure, but we regret neglecting something good; so pleasure isn't good or useful.
8.11: Ask of anything: what is it in itself, what is it made of, what causes it, what is it doing here, and how long will it last?
8.12: When you don't want to get out of bed, remember that serving others is your nature as a human, while sleeping is something animals do too.
8.13: With every impression, apply what you know about nature, ethics and logic.
8.14: Whenever you meet someone, ask what they believe is good and bad; then nothing they do will surprise you, because they're acting on those beliefs.
8.15: Being surprised by what the world produces is as silly as being surprised that a fig tree grows figs, or a doctor being surprised by a fever.
8.16: Changing your mind when someone corrects you is just as free an act as sticking to your mistake; the choice is still yours.
8.17: If it's up to you, why do it? If it's up to someone else, who are you blaming? Blame nobody: fix the cause if you can, fix the thing if you can't, and otherwise complaining is pointless.
8.18: What dies doesn't leave the universe; it changes and breaks down into elements, which keep changing too without complaining.
8.19: Everything exists for some purpose, a horse, a vine, even the sun; what is your purpose? Surely not just pleasure.
8.20: Nature cares about how things end as much as how they begin; a ball thrown up gains nothing going up and loses nothing coming down, and a bubble loses nothing when it bursts.
8.21: Look at the body inside out, when old, when sick; praiser and praised are both short-lived, in a tiny corner of a world that is itself a dot.
8.22: Focus on what's in front of you. You deserve this trouble, because you'd rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
8.23: When I act, I act for the good of people; when something happens to me, I accept it as coming from the gods and the source of everything.
8.24: Bathing is oil, sweat, dirt and filthy water; every part of life is like that if you look closely.
8.25: One person watches another die, then dies too; it's the same for everyone, even clever and famous people, all long gone. Your little self will also dissolve.
8.26: Doing what humans are made for brings satisfaction: being kind to others, resisting the senses, judging appearances clearly, and studying how the universe works.
8.27: You have three relationships: to your body, to the divine source of everything, and to the people you live with.
8.28: Pain is either the body's problem, so let it speak for itself, or the soul's, and the soul can keep its calm by refusing to call pain evil.
8.29: Wipe out false impressions by telling yourself: I can keep all badness, craving and disturbance out of my soul, see things for what they are, and use each for what it's worth.
8.30: Speak plainly and appropriately to everyone, in the senate or anywhere, without putting on airs.
8.31: Augustus's entire court is dead, and whole families end with 'the last of his line' on a tomb; all that effort to leave heirs, and someone has to be the last.
8.32: Build your life one action at a time; if each act does its job, be content. If something blocks you, accept it and switch to what you can do; another chance to act opens right away.
8.33: Accept wealth or success without arrogance, and be ready to let it go.
8.34: If you resent what happens or cut yourself off from others, you're like a severed hand; but unlike a hand, you can always reattach yourself to the whole.
8.35: Just as nature absorbs whatever stands against it and makes it part of itself, a rational being can turn any obstacle into material for its own goals.
8.36: Don't think about all of life's troubles at once; ask what about this moment is unbearable. Past and future can't hurt you, only the present, and it shrinks when you isolate it.
8.37: The mourners sitting at tombs died too, and even if the dead noticed, it wouldn't make them immortal; it's all just a bag of blood and stench.
8.38: If you can see clearly, look and judge wisely.
8.39: There's no virtue in a rational being that opposes justice, but there is one that opposes pleasure-seeking: self-control.
8.40: Remove your opinion about what seems painful and you're completely safe. Your reason doesn't have to trouble itself; let any other part that suffers speak for itself.
8.41: Pain and pleasure are for the senses to handle; an obstacle only harms your mind if you insisted on the outcome unconditionally. No fire, sword, tyrant or insult can touch the mind; once it's whole, it stays whole.
8.42: I shouldn't hurt myself, since I've never deliberately hurt anyone else.
8.43: Different people enjoy different things; my joy is keeping my mind sound, not turning away from anyone or anything, and welcoming it all.
8.44: Make the most of the present; people chasing posthumous fame forget that future people will be just as annoying and mortal as those around them now.
8.45: Throw me wherever you like; my inner self will stay calm. A change of place is no reason for my soul to shrink, swell or panic.
8.46: Nothing happens to anyone that isn't natural for them, as with an ox or a vine; so why complain? Nature brings nothing you can't bear.
8.47: If something outside you bothers you, it's not the thing but your judgment of it, and you can erase that judgment now. If you're upset about not doing what's right, act instead of complaining.
8.48: The mind is unbeatable when it withdraws into itself; a mind free of passions is a fortress, the safest refuge a person has.
8.49: Don't add anything to first impressions: you're told someone insulted you, not that you were harmed; your child is sick, not that their life is in danger. Stick to the facts and nothing has happened to you.
8.50: Bitter cucumber? Throw it out. Thorns on the path? Walk around them. Don't ask why such things exist; nature recycles everything, even what looks like waste.
8.51: Even if people kill or curse you, your mind can stay pure, like a clear spring that washes away the mud thrown into it. Keep your fountain flowing with freedom, contentment, simplicity and modesty.
8.52: If you don't know what the world is or what it's for, you don't know who you are; so why want praise from people who don't know where or who they are?
8.53: Do you want praise from someone who curses themselves constantly, or to please someone who isn't pleased with themselves?
8.54: Just as you breathe the air around you, let your mind take in the intelligence that fills everything; it's there for anyone who will draw it in.
8.55: Evil doesn't harm the universe, and one person's wrongdoing doesn't harm anyone else; it only harms the wrongdoer, who could drop it anytime.
8.56: My neighbor's choices don't affect my will any more than their body does; if their wickedness could harm me, my happiness would depend on them, and God didn't design it that way.
8.57: Let your mind shine like sunlight: spreading outward, steady, not crashing violently into obstacles but resting on them and lighting up whatever will receive it.
8.58: If you fear death, you fear either feeling nothing, in which case nothing can hurt you, or feeling something else, in which case you'll still be alive in another form.
8.59: People exist for one another, so teach them or put up with them.
8.60: The mind moves differently from an arrow, but even when it's cautious or exploring, it still moves straight toward its target.
8.61: Get inside other people's minds, and let them into yours.
9.1: Injustice, lying, chasing pleasure and fearing pain are all offenses against nature, which made us to help one another and treats pleasure and pain, life and death, with indifference.
9.2: Best to leave life never having tasted lies, hypocrisy, luxury and pride; next best to leave once you're sick of them. A corrupted mind is a worse plague than any disease.
9.3: Don't despise death; welcome it as one of nature's processes, like growing up, aging or giving birth. Wait for it the way you wait for a baby to arrive.
9.4: Whoever does wrong wrongs themselves, because they make themselves worse.
9.5: You can do wrong by not doing something, not just by doing something.
9.6: A clear-headed judgment right now, an action right now that serves others, and contentment right now with whatever happens: that's enough.
9.7: Erase false impressions, curb desire, quench cravings, and keep your mind in your own control.
9.8: Animals share one life, and rational beings share one mind, just as we all share one earth, one light and one air.
9.9: Like seeks like: earth falls to earth and fire rises to fire, and rational beings are drawn to one another so strongly that it's easier to find dirt untouched by dirt than a person cut off from people.
9.10: People, God and the universe all bear fruit in season; reason bears fruit for everyone and for itself.
9.11: If you can, correct wrongdoers by teaching them; if you can't, be patient with them. Even the gods are kind to such people.
9.12: Don't work like a victim or to be pitied or admired; focus only on acting or holding back as the common good requires.
9.13: Today I escaped all my troubles, or rather threw them out, because they weren't outside me but in my own opinions.
9.14: Everything is familiar, fleeting and cheap; life now is just as it was for the people we've buried.
9.15: Things exist outside us and form no judgments about themselves; it's our own mind that judges them.
9.16: For a rational, social being, good and evil lie in what you do, not in what happens to you.
9.17: For a thrown stone, falling isn't bad and rising wasn't good.
9.18: Look inside the minds of the people whose judgment you fear, and see what kind of judges they are, even of themselves.
9.19: Everything is changing, you included; you're constantly decaying, and so is the universe.
9.20: Leave another person's wrongdoing where it is.
9.21: Each stage of your life, childhood, youth, adulthood, ended in a kind of death, and none was anything to fear; the end of your whole life isn't either.
9.22: Examine your own mind to make it just, the universe's to remember you're part of it, and your neighbor's to see if they acted from ignorance, remembering their mind is like yours.
9.23: You're part of a social whole, so let every act serve social life; anything that doesn't tears your life apart and is a kind of mutiny.
9.24: Kids' squabbles and games, little souls carrying corpses around: that's all life is.
9.25: Look at what a thing really is, separate from its material, and figure out how long something like that can last.
9.26: You've suffered endlessly because you weren't satisfied with your mind simply doing what it's made to do. Enough.
9.27: When people blame, hate or slander you, look into their souls and see what they're like; you'll see their opinion isn't worth worrying about. Still be kind to them, because they're your friends by nature.
9.28: Whether the universe is ruled by a god or by chance, don't be ruled by chance yourself. Soon the earth will cover us, and change will roll on wave after wave; seeing that makes perishable things seem worthless.
9.29: Don't wait for a perfect world; do what's needed now, don't look around for an audience, and be satisfied when even the smallest thing goes well. Philosophy's work is simple and modest.
9.30: Look down from above at countless people living, voyaging, being born and dying; think how many don't know your name and how quickly praise turns to blame. Fame is worthless.
9.31: Stay calm about what comes from outside, and be just in what comes from within, acting for the common good.
9.32: Much of what troubles you exists only in your opinion; drop it and you'll have room to take in the whole universe, all of time, and how brief each life is.
9.33: Everything you see will soon perish, and so will those who watch it; the very old and the very young end up in the same place.
9.34: Look at the minds of people who praise or blame you, as if their souls were bare; it's absurd that they think their opinions can harm or help you.
9.35: Loss is just change, and nature delights in change; everything happens well and always has.
9.36: Everything's made of rotten stuff: water, dust, bones, filth; marble is hardened earth, gold is sediment, clothes are hair, purple dye is blood.
9.37: Enough of this whining and monkey business. What's new here? Look at it; there's nothing more to it. It makes no difference whether you study this for a hundred years or three.
9.38: If someone did wrong, the harm is theirs; and maybe they didn't do wrong at all.
9.39: Either everything comes from one intelligence and the part shouldn't complain about what helps the whole, or it's all atoms; either way, why be upset?
9.40: Instead of praying for things to happen or not happen, pray not to fear, crave or grieve over them: not 'let me keep my son' but 'let me not fear losing him'.
9.41: Like Epicurus, who kept discussing philosophy instead of his illness, stay focused on what you're doing and on keeping your mind calm, whatever happens to your body.
9.42: When someone's shamelessness offends you, ask: could the world be without shameless people? No, so don't demand the impossible. Nature gave us kindness to meet cruelty, and doing good is its own reward, like an eye seeing.
10.1: Will my soul ever be simple, whole and content, wanting nothing more, no longer craving pleasure, more time or better company, but satisfied with what it has and at peace with gods and people?
10.2: Figure out what your nature needs and do it, as long as it doesn't make you worse as a rational, social being; worry about nothing else.
10.3: Whatever happens, either you're built to bear it, so bear it without complaining, or you're not, and then it will end with you; and you can bear almost anything by deciding it's your interest or duty.
10.4: If someone is wrong, kindly show them their mistake; if you can't, blame yourself, or not even yourself.
10.5: Whatever happens to you was prepared from all eternity; the chain of causes has been spinning your thread since the beginning.
10.6: I'm part of a whole run by nature and related to other people; nothing that benefits the whole can harm a part, so I'll accept what I'm given and act for the common good, and life will flow happily.
10.7: Everything in the universe must change and break down, but that isn't evil; it's how the whole stays healthy, and our bodies were always just borrowed material in flux.
10.8: Once you've earned names like good, modest, truthful, rational, even-tempered and big-hearted, keep them, and get back to them fast if you slip; you'll be a new person. Do what a human is for, like a fig tree doing a fig tree's work.
10.9: Daily distractions, fights, fear, laziness and servility wear away your principles. Act in a way that sharpens practical skill and understanding, and know each thing for what it really is and how long it lasts.
10.10: A spider is proud of catching a fly, a man of catching a hare, a general of capturing enemies; look at their reasons and they're all just robbers.
10.11: Practice seeing how everything turns into something else; nothing builds greatness of mind more. Such a person ignores what others say, acts justly now and accepts what's given.
10.12: Why worry when you can figure out what to do? If the way is clear, take it without looking back; if not, stop and get good advice. Even if you fail, fail trying to do right.
10.13: When you wake up, ask: does it matter to me whether someone else does right? No. Remember what the people who arrogantly praise and blame are really like.
10.14: A wise, humble person says to nature, which gives and takes everything: give what you want, take back what you want, and means it gladly, not defiantly.
10.15: You don't have much life left; live it as if on a mountaintop. Let people see someone who truly lives by nature, and if they can't stand it, let them kill you.
10.16: Stop arguing about what a good person should be. Be one.
10.17: Keep the whole of time and matter in mind; any single thing is a fig seed in substance and a twist of a drill in time.
10.18: Look at anything that exists and see that it's already decaying and changing; everything is made to die.
10.19: Picture people eating, sleeping, having sex and using the toilet, then think of them strutting and scolding from on high; recently slaves to such things, and soon gone.
10.20: Whatever nature brings to something is good for it, and good at the moment it comes.
10.21: The earth loves rain and the universe loves making whatever is about to happen; I say to the universe, I love what you love.
10.22: Either you stay and you're used to it, you leave by choice, or you die having done your duty; there's nothing else, so cheer up.
10.23: Wherever you are is the same as a mountaintop or a beach; you can live in a city as peacefully as a shepherd on a hill.
10.24: Ask: what am I making of my mind right now, and what am I using it for? Is it thoughtless, cut off from others, or melted into my body's urges?
10.25: Running from your master makes you a runaway, and the law of the universe is the master; being angry, sad or afraid about what it assigns makes you a runaway too.
10.26: From a seed comes a child and from food come thought and strength; look at the hidden power that does this, unseen but as plain as gravity.
10.27: Things have always been this way and always will be; the courts of past emperors were the same play with different actors.
10.28: Someone who complains about what happens is like a pig kicking and squealing as it's sacrificed; everyone has to follow fate, but only rational beings can follow it willingly.
10.29: Whatever you're doing, stop and ask whether death is really terrible for taking this away.
10.30: When someone's fault offends you, think of your own similar faults, like valuing money, pleasure or reputation; your anger will fade, especially when you see they couldn't help it.
10.31: Whenever you see someone, think of someone like them who's dead; where are they now? Human affairs are smoke. Use the brief time you have to digest everything that happens, like fire turning whatever is thrown in into flame.
10.32: Don't let anyone truthfully say you're not honest or good; that's entirely up to you, so resolve not to live unless you are.
10.33: Whatever reason says is best, you can do or say, so stop making excuses. Treat acting by your nature as your pleasure; you can do it anywhere, and no misfortune harms you unless it harms the law of things.
10.34: People are like leaves: the wind scatters them and new ones grow. Your children, your critics and those who'd carry your fame are all leaves, so why chase or run from things as if they'd last forever?
10.35: A healthy eye sees everything, not just green things; a healthy mind is ready for whatever happens, not demanding 'let my children live and let everyone praise me.'
10.36: Even the best person will have someone at their deathbed glad to see them go; remembering that makes it easier to leave, gently and without dragging your feet.
10.37: Whenever someone does something, ask what they're aiming at; but start by asking it of yourself.
10.38: What pulls your strings is the hidden thing inside you: that's life, that's the person. Your body is just a tool, like an axe or a pen.
11.1: A rational soul sees itself, shapes itself, and enjoys its own fruit; unlike a play cut short, its life is complete whenever it ends. It surveys the whole universe and all of time, and loves its neighbor, truth and modesty.
11.2: Break a song into separate notes or a dance into separate moves and it loses its hold on you; do this with everything except virtue, and with life itself.
11.3: Admirable is the soul that's ready to leave the body at any moment, whatever comes after, as a reasoned choice made with dignity, not stubbornness or theatrics.
11.4: Did I do something for the common good? Then I've already been rewarded. Keep that in mind and keep doing good.
11.5: What's your profession? Being good. And you do it well by knowing how the universe works and what a human being is made for.
11.6: Tragedy reminds us that life's disasters are natural and bearable, and even comedy once taught humility; take the wisdom and ask what the whole show is for.
11.7: No situation in life is better suited to practicing philosophy than the one you're in right now.
11.8: A branch cut from its neighbor is cut from the whole tree; when you hate someone and turn away, you cut yourself off from all of society. You can regrow, but the more often you split off, the harder it gets.
11.9: Don't let people who block you push you off course, and don't let them push you out of kindness toward them; being irritated is as weak as giving up out of fear.
11.10: Nature is never inferior to art, and art makes lower things serve higher ones; that's where justice comes from, and justice fails if we care about trivial things or are careless and fickle.
11.11: You chase or run from things that don't come to you; quiet your judgments about them and they'll stay still, and so will you.
11.12: The soul is like a sphere: whole and stable when it doesn't reach out, shrink, scatter or collapse, but shines with the light that shows it the truth.
11.13: Someone despises me? That's their problem; mine is to not do anything contemptible. Someone hates me? I'll stay kind and gentle and ready to show them their mistake, without lecturing or showing off my patience.
11.14: People despise and flatter each other; they want to rise above each other and bow before each other.
11.15: Anyone who announces 'I'm going to be honest with you' is fake; real honesty shows in your eyes without saying it. Nothing is worse than a fake friendship.
11.16: You can live the best life if you're indifferent to things that don't matter; things don't create our opinions about them, we write them ourselves, and we can erase them.
11.17: Think about where each thing came from, what it's made of, what it will become, and that it won't be harmed by changing.
11.18: When someone offends you, remember: we're made for each other; people act from their beliefs; nobody errs willingly; you have faults too; you don't know their reasons; life is short; it's your anger that hurts you; and kindness is unbeatable when it's sincere.
11.19: Watch for four mental slips: needless thoughts, divisive thoughts, saying what you don't really think, and self-reproach that means your body's urges have beaten your better self.
11.20: Every element in your body stays where the universe puts it; it's strange that only your mind rebels against its place, when it's asked only to be just, self-controlled and content.
11.21: If you don't have one consistent aim in life, you can't be the same person throughout; make that aim the common good and all your actions will line up.
11.22: Remember the country mouse and the town mouse, and how anxious the town mouse was.
11.23: Socrates called popular opinions bogeymen, things to scare children.
11.24: The Spartans gave guests the shady seats at public shows and sat wherever they could themselves.
11.25: Socrates turned down a king's invitation because he didn't want to receive a favor he couldn't repay.
11.26: Keep in mind people from the past who lived virtuously.
11.27: Look at the sky each morning to remember the stars, which always do their work the same way, pure and unveiled.
11.28: Think of Socrates wearing an animal skin after his wife took his cloak, and how he answered friends who were embarrassed for him.
11.29: You can't teach others rules of reading and writing until you've learned to follow them, and that's even more true of life.
11.30: You're a slave; free speech isn't for you.
11.32: They'll curse virtue with harsh words.
11.33: Looking for figs in winter is madness, and so is longing for a child once they're gone.
11.34: When you kiss your child, whisper 'you might die tomorrow'; it's not a bad omen to name something natural, any more than talking about harvesting grain.
11.35: Unripe grape, ripe bunch, raisin: each is a change, not into nothing, but into what doesn't exist yet.
11.36: No one can steal your free will.
11.37: Learn the skill of deciding what to agree with; act with regard to circumstances, the common good and real value, avoid sensual craving, and don't avoid things outside your control.
11.38: This isn't a debate about trivia; it's about whether you're sane or not.
11.39: Socrates asked: do you want rational souls or irrational ones? Sound ones. Then why don't you seek them? We have them. Then why do you fight and quarrel?
12.1: Everything you're taking the long way to get, you can have now: let go of the past, trust the future to providence, and live the present with acceptance and justice. Don't fear dying; fear never having started to live.
12.2: God sees our minds stripped of the body; if you learn to see that way too, you'll stop fussing over clothes, houses and reputation.
12.3: You're a little body, a little breath and a mind, and only the mind is truly yours. Cut away what others do, your past and your worries about the future, live only the present, and you'll be at peace until death.
12.4: We love ourselves more than anyone, yet care more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves; we couldn't last a day saying every thought out loud.
12.5: If it seems unfair that even the best people are wiped out at death, trust that if it ought to be otherwise the gods would have arranged it; arguing with them assumes they're just.
12.6: Practice even what you think you can't do; your weak left hand grips the reins better than the right because it's trained to.
12.7: Think about the state you want to be in, body and soul, when death comes, and how short life is against the endless abyss of time.
12.8: Look at things stripped bare: the purpose of actions, what pain, pleasure, death and fame really are, that we cause our own distress, that no one can block us, and that everything is opinion.
12.9: Use your principles like a boxer using their fists, not a gladiator with a sword; the sword can be dropped, but your hands are always with you.
12.10: See what things really are by breaking them into their material, their form and their purpose.
12.11: What freedom a person has to do only what God would approve and to accept whatever God gives.
12.12: Don't blame the gods for what happens naturally, since they do no wrong, or people, since they only do wrong unintentionally; blame nobody.
12.13: It's ridiculous and naive to be surprised by anything that happens in life.
12.14: Either fate is fixed, a kind providence rules, or it's chaos. If fate, why resist? If providence, be worthy of help. If chaos, be glad you have a mind of your own in the storm; it can take your body but not your mind.
12.15: A lamp shines until it goes out; will the truth, justice and self-control in you go out before you do?
12.16: Before judging someone, ask if it's really wrong, and whether they've already condemned themselves; expecting bad people not to do wrong is like expecting figs without juice or babies not to cry.
12.17: If it's not right, don't do it; if it's not true, don't say it.
12.18: Whenever something makes an impression, break it down into its form, its matter, its purpose and how long it will last.
12.19: Realize you have something better inside you than the passions that jerk you around like a puppet; ask what's in your mind right now: fear, suspicion, desire?
12.20: First, don't act at random or without purpose. Second, aim every action at the common good.
12.21: Soon you'll be nobody and nowhere, and so will everything and everyone you see now; everything is made to change and perish so new things can exist.
12.22: Everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power; drop it whenever you like and, like a sailor rounding the cape, you'll find calm water and a still harbor.
12.23: An action that ends at its proper time suffers no harm, and neither does a life that ends when nature decides; what serves the whole is always good and well-timed.
12.24: Keep three things ready: act justly and don't blame chance or providence for what happens; remember how every being comes and goes; and look down on human life from above to see how repetitive and brief it is.
12.25: Throw out your opinion and you're saved. Who's stopping you?
12.26: When you're upset, you've forgotten that everything follows nature, others' wrongs aren't yours, it's all happened before, we're all kin through reason, nothing is really yours, everything is opinion, and you only ever lose the present.
12.27: Remember the people who were famous, furious or unlucky; where are they now? Smoke, ash, a story or not even that. Be just, temperate and humble simply, because pride in your humility is the worst kind.
12.28: People ask how I know the gods exist; I've never seen my own soul either, but I honor it, and I know the gods from experiencing their power.
12.29: Life is secure when you understand what each thing is, act justly with your whole soul and speak the truth; then just enjoy linking one good deed to the next without gaps.
12.30: There's one sunlight split by walls and mountains, one substance in countless bodies, and one mind that seems divided; minds naturally seek one another and stay connected.
12.31: Do you want to keep living just to feel, grow and talk? If those aren't worth much, focus on following reason and God, and don't be troubled that death takes the rest.
12.32: You get a tiny sliver of endless time, of all matter and of the universal mind, and you crawl on a small clod of earth; so nothing is great except acting by your nature and accepting what nature brings.
12.33: How is your mind using itself? That's everything; the rest is ash and smoke.
12.34: Even people who think pleasure is good and pain is bad have looked down on death, which should help you not fear it.
12.35: For someone who thinks only well-timed things are good, and doesn't care whether they get more or fewer good deeds or years, death holds no terror.
12.36: You've been a citizen of the world; what does it matter if for five years or three? Nature, who brought you in, is sending you out, like an actor dismissed after three acts. Three acts can be the whole play, so leave content.
